analysis.one_liner: Creates the first federal licensing and reserve rules for dollar-pegged stablecoin issuers, shielding them from securities laws.
analysis.headline: Introduced with four Senate cosponsors in February 2025, the bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and has had no markup or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let only approved issuers — bank subsidiaries, federally approved nonbank companies, or state-approved firms — issue payment stablecoins, which are digital tokens pegged one-to-one to the U.S. dollar. Issuers would have to hold cash or short-term Treasury reserves equal to every coin outstanding, publish monthly reserve reports, and give stablecoin holders first claim on assets if the issuer goes bankrupt. At the same time, the bill shields these coins from securities laws, lets issuers under $10 billion choose lighter state oversight, and stops regulators from applying big-bank capital rules to the new issuers.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and prospective stablecoin issuers gain the biggest prize: a legal charter, official legitimacy, freedom from securities-law exposure, and lighter-than-bank treatment on capital, with automatic approval if regulators miss their 120-day review deadline. Large banks gain a new product line, since they could issue stablecoins through subsidiaries and would be barred from holding much capital against custody assets. People who hold or might hold stablecoins also gain real protections: guaranteed one-to-one reserves in cash or short-term Treasuries, monthly public reserve reports with criminal penalties for false certifications, segregated customer custody, and first priority in bankruptcy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Stablecoin issuers, big banks, and coin holders

how_it_helps.text: Issuers must back every stablecoin with one-to-one reserves in U.S. currency, insured deposits, short-term Treasury bills, or similarly liquid assets, so holders are not relying on nothing.
Issuers must publicly disclose their redemption policy and publish their reserve composition every month, with the CEO and CFO personally certifying accuracy under penalty of criminal law.
If a stablecoin issuer goes under, holders get first priority over every other creditor claim, including in bankruptcy court.
Issuers are treated as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, bringing anti-money-laundering and sanctions rules to a business that has operated largely offshore or in a gray zone.
Companies holding customers' stablecoins must keep customer assets segregated from their own and protected from their creditors, and only supervised firms may offer custody at all.
Only approved issuers may issue payment stablecoins in the United States, giving the market a single legal doorway instead of an ad hoc patchwork.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state regulators would bear the cost of examining and supervising a new class of issuers. The broader financial system and taxpayers bear residual risk: stablecoin holders are not covered by deposit insurance, the bill creates no government backstop, and because reserves must sit heavily in short-term Treasuries, a run on a large issuer could force fire sales that shake short-term funding markets. The public also gives up stricter alternatives — issuers escape securities-law oversight, face capital requirements capped at the minimum regulators judge sufficient, and are exempted from the Dodd-Frank bank-capital standard that applies to banks holding similar assets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Regulators, and the financial system if issuers fail

drawbacks.text: The bill amends five federal securities laws to declare permitted stablecoins are not securities, removing the SEC from oversight of a large new class of digital financial products.

Capital requirements for issuers 'may not exceed what is sufficient' for ongoing operations, and the bill expressly exempts issuers from section 171 of the Financial Stability Act of 2010 — the Dodd-Frank standard that applies to banks — so stablecoin issuers would be held to a lighter capital standard than banks holding the same assets.

Regulators must decide on applications within 120 days or the application is deemed approved, and may deny one only on safety-and-soundness grounds, sharply limiting their discretion to screen out risky operators.
Issuers with up to $10 billion outstanding may choose state regulation instead of federal supervision, recreating a patchwork of 50 potential rulebooks for a nationally traded product.

Stablecoin holders get bankruptcy priority but no deposit insurance and no lender of last resort; if a large issuer lost confidence, holders would depend on the issuer selling its Treasury holdings quickly, and no federal framework can guarantee redemptions in a panic.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and would make holding a stablecoin meaningfully safer than today's gray market: one-to-one reserves, monthly audited disclosure, custody segregation, and first claim in bankruptcy. But the framework is calibrated to issuer convenience. It grants securities-law immunity, caps capital requirements, exempts issuers from the bank-capital standard Congress passed after 2008, forces automatic approval of applications if regulators dawdle, and lets mid-sized issuers pick their own state regulator. The result is a permanent, private, uninsured payments system built on short-term government debt — safer than the status quo for holders, but with run and systemic risk that the bill acknowledges in its own reporting requirements without actually addressing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it, so it sits waiting while Congress continues.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Hagerty introduced the GENIUS Act on February 4, 2025, joined by Sens. Tim Scott of South Carolina, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, and Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming — two Republicans and two Democrats.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee has taken no action on the bill since referral — no markup, no vote, no floor action — and the Congress runs through January 2027, so the bill remains pending.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed for anyone: the bill sits in committee, stablecoin issuers keep operating under the existing patchwork of state rules and enforcement actions, and neither the industry nor holders have gained or lost from this bill. Its main effect to date is to put a stablecoin framework on the Senate's agenda in a form written around issuer preferences.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so the partisan split is unknown; sponsorship was evenly bipartisan, with two of 55 Senate Republicans and two of 45 Senate Democrats signing on.

industries.note: The bill makes approved private issuers the permanent, legally recognized channel for digital dollars and writes the rules around their preferences: no securities-law exposure, capital requirements capped at the minimum, exemption from bank capital rules, and automatic approval if regulators miss deadlines. Holders gain reserve, disclosure, and bankruptcy protections, but the framework entrenches a private, uninsured alternative to insured bank deposits as the payment rail of the future.

industries.industry: Large banks and insured depository institutions
industries.note: Banks may issue stablecoins through subsidiaries and the bill bars regulators from counting custody assets as liabilities or requiring significant capital against them, opening a new fee business with limited balance-sheet cost. Banks entering the market would compete with existing issuers while lending the system credibility.

The bill defines who may hold customers' stablecoins and keys, legitimizing the custody business under bank, federal, or state supervision in exchange for segregation and customer-protection rules. Clarity of this kind is what the industry has lobbied for, and it reduces the legal risk that has kept some institutions out of crypto.

Reserves must consist largely of Treasury bills of 93 days or less and related instruments, so every dollar of stablecoin growth creates structural demand for short-term government debt. This helps finance the federal deficit but ties the crypto payments system's safety to Treasury market liquidity in a crisis.

analysis.trajectory: Stablecoin legislation carries unusual bipartisan sponsorship — two Senate Republicans and two Senate Democrats — and active leadership interest, so a framework like this is more likely than not to reach the Senate floor in some form this Congress. This exact bill, however, has sat untouched since referral and is likely to be overtaken by a Banking Committee draft; the fight, when it comes, will be over oversight of nonbank issuers, capital and reserve rules, and whether large tech and bank issuers face extra conditions.
